newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa budgets for 4.0 pct deficit in 1997/98.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa budgets for 4.0 pct deficit in 1997/98.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said on Wednesday the government would achieve its target of a deficit before borrowing of 4.0 percent of GDP in 1997/98 by keeping a tight rein on expenditure.

Unveiling his annual budget, Manuel said total revenue was expected to increase by 11.1 percent to 161.976 billion rand in the year to March 31, 1998, equivalent to 26.0 percent of GDP, as in 1996/97.
But expenditure would rise only 6.1 percent to 186.747 billion rand, equivalent to 30.0 percent of GDP against 31.4 percent in 1996/97.
In real terms, government spending will fall by more than two percent with inflation expected to average 8.5 percent in the next budget year.
South Africa will have a budget deficit of 24.771 billion rand, 5.491 billion rand lower than the comparable revised estimated deficit for 1996/97.
The deficit in 1996/97 is expected to total 5.1 percent of GDP, or 5.4 percent before taking into account proceeds from asset sales.
"Unlike previous years when extraordinary revenues were included in the calculation of the deficit, for 1997/98 we have only considered ordinary revenue in the calculation," Manuel said.
After taking into account loan redemptions of 12 billion rand, South Africa's gross borrowing requirement will be 36.849 billion rand against 41.020 billion in 1996/97.

The bulk of this will be met by the issue of 27.702 billion rand of government stock, down from 34.241 billion in 1996/97, but the authorities also plan to increase their overseas borrowings by issuing 4.00 billion rand of foreign bonds against 2.83 billion in 1996/97.
Borrowing needs will also be reduced by the sale of strategic oil stocks which will net the government 1.25 billion rand.

On privatisation, Manuel took a conservative line, making no major provisions for receipts in cutting the 1997/98 borrowing requirement, apart from 516 million rand earned from the sale of six radio stations last year by the state broadcaster.
However, the government reiterated that redemption of state debts was one of the areas that would be addressed in using proceeds from the sale of state assets.

South Africa plans to conclude its first major privatisation deal next month with the sale of a 30 percent stake in telecommunication utility Telkom to a U.S.-Malaysian consortium. Analysts estimate the sale could net the government some six billion rand, some of which would go to enhance infrastructure and some to cut state debt.
Total government debt is projected to be 340.751 billion rand, or 54.8 percent of GDP, on March 31, 1998, compared to the estimated 309.507 billion rand, or 55.3 percent of GDP, on March 31, 1997.
